Starch.abstract: The main carbohydrate of rice, wheat and other grains, made of two kinds of glucose chain: amylose and amylopectin. Cooking with water makes it swell and gel; on cooling it slowly re-hardens (staling).

Amylose.abstract: The linear form of starch: glucose units joined in long, mostly unbranched chains. Rice with more amylose cooks firmer and less sticky.

Amylopectin.abstract: The branched form of starch. Glutinous rice, used for mochi, is almost pure amylopectin; the length of its chains affects how fast mochi hardens.

Glycogen.abstract: The storage carbohydrate of animal muscle. After a fish dies its muscle breaks glycogen down, using up ATP and producing lactic acid, so the pH falls.

Agarose.abstract: The neutral, gelling fraction of agar (kanten). It forms physical gels held together only by hydrogen bonds between its chains.

Agaropectin.abstract: The sulfated, non-gelling fraction of agar (kanten); like agarose, a polymer of agarobiose.

Gluten.abstract: The protein network that forms when wheat flour is mixed with water, built from gliadins and glutenins. Buckwheat has none, so soba dough needs other binders.

Gliadin.abstract: One of the two wheat proteins that form gluten; in dough, gliadins give viscosity.

Glutenin.abstract: One of the two wheat proteins that form gluten; in dough, glutenins give elasticity.

Globulins.abstract: Salt-soluble proteins; the main proteins of buckwheat, which do not form gluten.

Myosin.abstract: A contractile muscle protein. When ATP runs low after death it binds to actin; enzymes later break down its heavy chain, softening the flesh.

Actin.abstract: A contractile muscle protein that binds to myosin when ATP runs out after death (rigor).

Amylase.abstract: Enzymes that break starch into sugars such as glucose and oligosaccharides. Kōji mould produces them in large amounts.

Protease.abstract: Enzymes that break proteins into peptides and amino acids, releasing the glutamate behind umami. Kōji mould produces them in large amounts.

Glutaminase.abstract: An enzyme that turns glutamine into glutamate. Kōji strains with high glutaminase give soy sauce mash with more glutamate.

Ribonuclease.abstract: An enzyme that breaks down RNA. In shiitake it releases the umami nucleotide GMP, working best at 60–70 °C.

Nucleotidase.abstract: An enzyme that destroys GMP, turning it into guanosine, which is not umami; in shiitake it works best at 45–50 °C.

Carboxypeptidase.abstract: Enzymes that cut amino acids from the ends of peptides. In soy sauce mash, acid-loving carboxypeptidases keep releasing glutamate as the pH falls.

Lipoxygenase.abstract: Enzymes that oxidise fats; the lipoxygenase pathway drives the deterioration of stored buckwheat flour.

Tyrosinase.abstract: An enzyme that makes brown pigments. Kōji strains with high tyrosinase activity are avoided where a bright colour is wanted.

Polyphenols.abstract: A large class of plant compounds. Water-soluble polyphenols in adzuki bean skins would turn bean paste brown, so the cooking water is discarded.

Anthocyanins.abstract: Water-soluble plant pigments (red, purple, blue). The purple pigments of adzuki beans are different: almost insoluble in water.

Proanthocyanidins.abstract: Colourless polyphenols, abundant in adzuki bean seed coats, that oxidise to yellow-brown compounds.

Melanoidins.abstract: Brown polymers produced by the Maillard reaction between amino compounds and sugars; they give soy sauce and miso their colour.

Fatty acids.abstract: The building blocks of fats. Free fatty acids accumulate as stored buckwheat flour deteriorates.

Peroxides.abstract: Oxidation products of fats; they increase as stored buckwheat flour deteriorates.
